analysis.title: Expanding Our Market Cycle Framework
key_insights: Morgan Stanley updated its US market cycle framework for the first time since 2019. It uses macro, credit and corporate data to classify the market into four phases: Early Advance, Mature Advance, Defensive Shift and Market Stress. The indicator currently reads "Mature Advance".

The indicator entered Mature Advance in May 2025, after holding Defensive Shift since February 2023. It troughed in October 2024 and now sits near a four-year high. 7 of the 10 components are strengthening over six months, close to the best breadth since the post-Covid reopening.

Historically, Mature Advance has favored equities over fixed income. US stocks beat US HY by 3.1 percentage points more than their typical margin, and Europe by 4.6 points. Equities also beat government bonds by more than usual: S&P 500 by about 1 point vs USTs, MSCI Europe by about 3 vs Bunds, FTSE 100 by about 2 vs gilts, Topix by about 4 vs JGBs.

Within equities, Mature Advance favors DM over EM (EM lags) and large caps over small. This underpins the team's preference for DM over EM equities this year. Energy prices and trade tensions have added to EM headwinds. US equity strategists expect large-cap and quality leadership to persist.

In Mature Advance, only equities and the dollar get a consistent boost in absolute returns. Government bonds, credit and commodities return close to or below their long-run averages. IG excess returns are near average and HY is moderately below.

AI capex could push equity returns above the framework's historical norms. US equity strategists see total AI investment at $1.6 trillion in 2027, about two-thirds flowing to S&P 500 companies as revenue. They expect 25% earnings growth for AI enablers and adopters, which would account for 78% of S&P earnings growth in 2027.

Fed hikes have often preceded turns to Defensive Shift: 8 of 11 past Mature Advance to Defensive Shift turns followed a net rise in Fed funds over the prior 12 months, averaging +95 bp. AI capex is relatively macro-indifferent, so the usual link between hikes and a Defensive turn may not hold even if the economists' expected hikes arrive.

Defensive Shift is only a modest drag on risk assets. The S&P 500 has averaged about 11% forward 12M returns and MSCI EM 12%. Japan equities underperform their average by 3.7 points. US and European HY excess returns are 3.0 and 5.2 points below long-run averages, so most credit gains come from duration.

In Defensive Shift, USTs and UKTs roughly match their averages while DBRs and JGBs lag by more than 1 point. The DXY runs about 1 point below its average, and EUR and JPY gain about 2 points above typical levels against USD. Gold has jumped about 9% in past Defensive episodes.

Around the Mature Advance to Defensive Shift turn, US stocks beat EM equities by 11 points and Japanese equities by 8 points versus average. They also beat USTs and DBRs by 1-2 points more than usual. The shift is toward quality, not a broad exit from risk.

The real risk is the transition to Market Stress, with only five episodes in the history. The S&P 500 fell 38% peak-to-trough on average as the indicator entered the phase. Individual drawdowns were 19% in 1990, 44% in 2000-02, 55% in 2007-09 and 34% in 2020. US HY excess returns fell 39% in 2008 and 23% in 2020, and copper fell about 23%.

Over those drawdown windows, 7-10Y USTs returned about 18% on average, front-end USTs about 9%, DBRs about 12% and gold about 12%. Around the Market Stress turn, USTs beat the S&P 500 by about 31% more than usual, EM equities by about 32% and MSCI Europe by about 39%.

Most Defensive regimes return to Mature Advance rather than sliding into Market Stress. Because the data are backward-looking, equities and credit bottom about 3-5 months after entry into Market Stress, and later months flatter the phase's average returns.

Method changes in v2026: five of ten components are replaced. Dropped are Conference Board confidence, 2s10s curve, ISM manufacturing production, real estate loans and financial bond issuance. Added are the Chicago Fed nonfinancial leverage index, PCE durable goods inflation, manufacturer's inventory/sales ratio, housing units under construction and T12M stock issuance. Z-scores now use a rolling 10-year window instead of full history.

Phase classification: the level is the average z-score against its long-run trailing midpoint. Rate of change is improving if 60% or more of components strengthen over six months, and deteriorating if 60% or more weaken.
Portfolio stance: stay overweight global equities over fixed income, favoring US equities over the rest of the world.

macro_indicators.reading: Economists expect more Fed hikes; the Fed is described as embarking on a hiking cycle
macro_indicators.interpretation: Hikes have preceded most turns to Defensive Shift, but AI capex may break that link and risk assets could weather the shift.

macro_indicators.indicator: Fed funds net change before Defensive Shift turns
macro_indicators.reading: +95 bp average over the prior 12 months across 11 episodes
macro_indicators.interpretation: Historical average that gives context for how often hikes coincide with a turn to Defensive Shift.
About two-thirds should flow to S&P 500 companies as revenue and support equity returns beyond the framework's historical norms.

macro_indicators.indicator: AI enabler and adopter earnings growth
macro_indicators.interpretation: These firms are on track to account for 78% of S&P earnings growth in 2027.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight global equities versus fixed income, favoring US equities over the rest of the world
trade_ideas.rationale: Mature Advance historically favors equities over fixed income, and AI capex adds support, especially in the US.
trade_ideas.risk: A turn to Market Stress would see risk assets sell off sharply and duration outperform.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight DM equities over EM equities, and large caps over small caps
trade_ideas.rationale: Mature Advance sees DM outperform EM and large caps outperform small caps. EM faces energy price and trade headwinds.
trade_ideas.risk: Not stated beyond the transition risks.

risk_factors: A transition to Market Stress has historically brought severe drawdowns in equities, credit and copper, while duration and gold rally.
Fed hikes tighten financial conditions and have preceded most turns to Defensive Shift, with credit growth slowing and corporate capital markets activity pulling back.
Defensive Shift brings below-average HY excess returns, and Japan equities underperform their average.
The indicator relies on backward-looking economic data that tend to bottom after risk markets do.
geopolitical: The report cites trade tensions and higher energy prices as headwinds for EM equities this cycle.

tension_points.bull_case: Even if the Fed hikes as MS economists expect, AI capex is relatively macro-indifferent, so the usual link to a Defensive turn may not hold. Even in Defensive Shift, the S&P 500 has averaged about 11% forward 12M returns.
tension_points.bear_case: Eight of 11 past turns to Defensive Shift followed Fed hikes averaging 95 bp. Tighter conditions slow credit growth and risk assets lose momentum.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A transition from Defensive Shift into Market Stress, which has brought an average 38% S&P 500 peak-to-trough drawdown.

theme_stances.key_argument: Mature Advance is the best phase for equities to beat HY credit, and stocks also beat government bonds by more than usual.
theme_stances.evidence: Mature Advance has historically favored equities over fixed income

theme_stances.key_argument: AI capex spending could push equity returns above historical norms, especially in the US.
theme_stances.evidence: equities could very well see even stronger returns than our framework suggests
